WAGE THEFT PREVENTION ACT NOTICE TO EMPLOYEE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

ABOUT THIS WAGE THEFT PREVENTION ACT NOTICE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the written hiring-time notice that California Labor Code § 2810.5 requires many employers to give many new employees, in connection with Acme Manufacturing, Inc.'s hiring of Morgan T. Ellis with a start date of April 1, 2026. It summarizes selected requirements of that statute: who the statute's notice duty reaches and does not reach, what categories of information the notice must contain, and the separate duty to notify an employee in writing of later changes to that information. It is not the Labor Commissioner's own "Notice to Employee" template, does not itself serve as the written notice the statute requires, and does not state, verify, or determine Morgan T. Ellis's actual pay rate, payday, exempt or non-exempt status, or any other term of Morgan T. Ellis's employment with Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

THE HIRING-TIME WRITTEN NOTICE REQUIREMENT
California law requires an employer to give each employee a written notice at the time of hiring, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to that employee, containing a specified list of categories of information. Acme Manufacturing, Inc.'s hiring of Morgan T. Ellis falls within the timing this statute describes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "At the time of hiring, an employer shall provide to each employee a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, containing the following information:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, hiring-time written notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)), used as real evidence of California's hiring-time written-notice requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's actual situation. The statute's own definition of "employee" for this section excludes several categories of workers, described in a separate clause of this information sheet; this clause states only the general notice duty and does not by itself establish that any particular worker is or is not within the statute's coverage. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific notice given (or not given) by any particular employer complied with Section 2810.5, and does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with it.

CATEGORIES OF INFORMATION THE NOTICE MUST CONTAIN
The statute lists specific categories of information the hiring-time notice must contain, including the employee's rate or rates of pay and the basis for that rate (such as hourly, shift, day, week, salary, piece, or commission, including any overtime rate), any allowances claimed as part of the minimum wage, the regular payday, the employer's name (including any "doing business as" names), the employer's physical and mailing address, the employer's telephone number, the name, address, and telephone number of the employer's workers' compensation insurance carrier, specified information about paid sick leave rights, specified information about certain recent federal or state emergency or disaster declarations affecting the county of employment, and any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The rate or rates of pay and basis thereof, whether paid by the hour, shift, day, week, salary, piece, commission, or otherwise, including any rates for overtime, as applicable."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, rate(s) of pay and basis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "Allowances, if any, claimed as part of the minimum wage, including meal or lodging allowances."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, minimum-wage allowances (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "The regular payday designated by the employer in accordance with the requirements of this code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, regular payday (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "The name of the employer, including any “doing business as” names used by the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer name and DBAs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "The physical address of the employer’s main office or principal place of business, and a mailing address, if different."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(E) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer physical and mailing address (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "The telephone number of the employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(F) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer telephone number (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "The name, address, and telephone number of the employer’s workers’ compensation insurance carrier."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(G) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, workers' compensation carrier information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "That an employee: may accrue and use sick leave; has a right to request and use accrued paid sick leave; may not be terminated or retaliated against for using or requesting the use of accrued paid sick leave; and has the right to file a complaint against an employer who retaliates."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(H) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, paid sick leave rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "The existence of a federal or state emergency or disaster declaration applicable to the county or counties where the employee is to be employed, and that was issued within 30 days before the employee’s first day of employment, that may affect their health and safety during their employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(I) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, emergency or disaster declaration disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "Any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(J) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner catch-all (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(A)-(J)), used as real evidence of what California's hiring-time notice must contain — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All ten citations below are to subparagraphs (A) through (J) of a single statutory paragraph, Section 2810.5(a)(1); they are treated here as one source describing one list, not as independent corroborating sources. Two of these required categories — subparagraph (H), on paid sick leave rights, and subparagraph (I), on certain recent emergency or disaster declarations — are easy to omit from an informal summary of this statute because they were added by later amendments rather than appearing in the section's original 2011 enactment; this clause's drafter confirms both are present in the current, amended text quoted below. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific notice given (or not given) by any particular employer included every required category, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

EMPLOYEES THE STATUTE'S DEFINITION EXCLUDES
For purposes of this notice requirement, the statute defines "employee" to exclude three categories of workers: an employee directly employed by the state or a political subdivision of the state (such as a city, county, city and county, or special district); an employee who is exempt from the payment of overtime wages by statute or by an Industrial Welfare Commission wage order; and an employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours, and working conditions and that meets specified premium overtime-pay and minimum regular-hourly-rate conditions set out in the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For purposes of this section, “employee” does not include any of the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition-of-employee introductory clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "An employee directly employed by the state or any political subdivision thereof, including any city, county, city and county, or special district."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, state and political-subdivision employees excluded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "An employee who is exempt from the payment of overtime wages by statute or the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, overtime-exempt employees excluded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "An employee who is covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement if the agreement expressly provides for the wages, hours of work, and working conditions of the employee, and if the agreement provides premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked and a regular hourly rate of pay for those employees of not less than 30 percent more than the state minimum wage."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, qualifying collective-bargaining-agreement employees excluded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(c)), used as real evidence of which categories of workers this particular notice statute's own definition excludes — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that a collective-bargaining agreement covering any particular reader does or does not meet the specific premium-pay and minimum-rate conditions the statute sets out. All four citations below are to the introductory clause and paragraphs (1) through (3) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 2810.5(c); they are treated here as one source describing one exclusion list, not as independent corroborating sources. The third exclusion is narrower than a blanket exemption for any employee covered by any collective bargaining agreement: the statute requires the agreement itself to expressly address wages, hours, and working conditions, and to provide a premium overtime rate and a regular hourly rate at least 30 percent above the state minimum wage; this clause does not determine whether any specific collective bargaining agreement meets that test. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular individual worker falls inside or outside this statute's definition of "employee," and does not determine that any particular employer's notice practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

DUTY TO NOTIFY EMPLOYEES IN WRITING OF LATER CHANGES
Separately from the hiring-time notice itself, the statute requires an employer to notify its employees in writing of any changes to the information set forth in the notice, within seven calendar days after the time of the change, unless the change is reflected on a timely wage statement furnished to the employee, or is provided in another writing the employer is otherwise required by law to give the employee within seven days of the change.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall notify their employees in writing of any changes to the information set forth in the notice within seven calendar days after the time of the changes, unless one of the following applies:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, seven-day update notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "All changes are reflected on a timely wage statement furnished in accordance with Section 226."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, timely-wage-statement exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "Notice of all changes is provided in another writing required by law within seven days of the changes."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, other-required-writing exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(b)), used as real evidence of California's update-notice requirement and its two stated exceptions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All three citations below are to the introductory clause and paragraphs (1) and (2) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 2810.5(b); they are treated here as one source describing one requirement and its exceptions, not as independent corroborating sources. The seven-calendar-day period runs from the time of the change itself, not from when the employer discovers or acts on it, and the statute measures it in calendar days rather than business days. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific update notice given (or not given) by any particular employer, or any specific wage statement, satisfied this requirement, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5(b).

LABOR COMMISSIONER TEMPLATE, AND ADDITIONAL CONTENT FOR TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYERS
The statute directs the Labor Commissioner to prepare templates for the required hiring-time notice and to make those templates available to employers. Separately, if the employer is a "temporary services employer" as statutorily defined, the notice must also include the name, physical and mailing address, and telephone number of the client legal entity for which the employee will actually perform work, along with any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary — a requirement that itself does not apply to a security services company licensed by the Department of Consumer Affairs that solely provides security services.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The Labor Commissioner shall prepare templates for the required notices that comply with the requirements of paragraphs (1) and (4). The templates shall be made available to employers in a manner as determined by the Labor Commissioner, and as set forth in subdivision (d)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner template requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  "If the employer is a temporary services employer, as defined in Section 201.3, the notice described in paragraph (1) shall also include the name, the physical address of the main office, the mailing address if different from the physical address of the main office, and the telephone number of the legal entity for whom the employee will perform work, and any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer additional content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(2) and (a)(3)), used as real evidence that a Labor Commissioner template exists and that temporary services employers face an additional content requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Section 2810.5(a); they are treated here as one source describing two related administrative provisions, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause does not reproduce the Labor Commissioner's template itself and did not fetch or verify the template document's current content or web location; it relies only on the statutory text's own description that such a template must be prepared and made available. The statute also contains a further, separate content requirement for notices given to employees admitted under the federal H-2A agricultural visa program, in Section 2810.5(a)(4); that H-2A-specific provision is not quoted or summarized in this clause, an honest gap disclosed rather than covered. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer is or is not a "temporary services employer" as the statute defines that term, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

NO PENALTY PROVISION SPECIFIC TO THIS SECTION FOUND IN ITS OWN TEXT
The text of Labor Code § 2810.5 itself, in subdivisions (a) through (d), does not state a civil penalty, fine, or other sanction tied specifically to an employer's failure to provide the hiring-time notice or the update notice the section describes. Two other California Labor Code sections that create civil penalties for related pay-practice failures — Section 1197.1, addressing paying an employee less than the applicable minimum wage, and Section 226.3, addressing failure to provide a compliant itemized wage statement or to keep required payroll records — do not, in their current codified text, name Section 2810.5 or its hiring-time or update-notice requirements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any employer or other person acting either individually or as an officer, agent, or employee of another person, who pays or causes to be paid to any employee a wage less than the minimum fixed by an applicable state or local law, or by an order of the commission, shall be subject to a civil penalty, restitution of wages, liquidated damages payable to the employee, and any applicable penalties imposed pursuant to Section 203 as follows:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, minimum-wage civil penalty (no reference to Section 2810.5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.1.)
  "Any employer who violates subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall be subject to a civil penalty in the amount of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per employee per violation in an initial citation and one thousand dollars ($1,000) per employee for each violation in a subsequent citation, for which the employer fails to provide the employee a wage deduction statement or fails to keep the records required in subdivision (a) of Section 226."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.3 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, wage-statement/recordkeeping civil penalty (no reference to Section 2810.5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text, used as real evidence that these three specific sections do not on their face state a penalty tied to Section 2810.5 — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that no California law of any kind provides any consequence for a failure to give this notice. This clause's drafter checked only these three sections (2810.5 itself, 1197.1, and 226.3) directly against their current statutory text; it did not exhaustively check every other Labor Code provision that could conceivably bear on enforcement, such as the Labor Commissioner's general citation and hearing authority under Section 98, or a representative action under the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act — an honest gap, disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. An absence found across three checked sections is evidence of an absence, not proof that no enforcement mechanism exists anywhere in California law for a Section 2810.5 violation. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's failure (or compliance) has any particular legal consequence, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you received this information sheet.

Employee: Morgan T. Ellis
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme Manufacturing, Inc.:
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________
